name: Ben Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and won't be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Millbrook Family Practice, in a market town about forty minutes out of the city. It's six doctors, a lot of farmers and retired people, and Dr Halvorsen, the senior partner, who still keeps a paper diary for home visits. I do morning surgery, about sixteen patients, then visits in the afternoon, mostly older people who can't get in. I'm slower than I should be, and the computer system still beats me most days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you going, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The home visits keep me going. You sit in someone's kitchen and you learn more in five minutes than in a fifteen-minute appointment. What wears me down is the screen and the forms, and people expecting me to know everything when I've been qualified about five minutes. My girlfriend Lucia is a pharmacist at the chemist on the high street, so half the town knows us both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Every couple of years there's a new thing that's going to change medicine, and then it's mostly another login. I wouldn't post about it, I don't really post, but I'd say it over a pint after football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me. I never use those tools anyway, so nothing changes for me. Job's safe, pay's decent, Lucia and I have savings, and there are always practices looking for doctors around here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, basically. Finish my specialist training, learn the computer system properly, keep doing the visits. Lucia and I are saving for a house deposit over the next two years, so we'd carry on putting money aside for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Relieved, a bit. Nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the computer system beats you most days. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week I spent ten minutes trying to find where to send a blood test request while a farmer sat there with his cap in his hands. Dr Halvorsen just laughed and did it on paper. I can do the medicine, mostly, it's the screens I'm slow on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about Millbrook that worries you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dr Halvorsen retires in two years, and he's the one I ask when I'm stuck. When our senior doctor retires, I lose my safety net, whatever happens with AI. That worries me more than any computer.

say: I'm **not surprised**, because every new medical tool ends up as another login.
I'd say it over a **pint after football**, not online.
think: It **suits me**, since I never use those tools anyway.
My **job, pay and savings** are safe, and nearby practices always need doctors.
do: Finish my **specialist training** and keep doing home visits.
Learn the practice's **computer system** properly at last.
Keep saving with Lucia for a **house deposit** over two years.
feel: **Relieved** and settled, with nothing to lose sleep over.
S0.quote: When our senior doctor retires, I lose my safety net, whatever happens with AI.
fieldNote: His real worry is the **senior partner retiring**, not technology.
He struggles with **screens**, not medicine, and says so with some embarrassment.
He sounds **content** in a world where little changes.

steps.text: Keep doing afternoon home visits and finish specialist training
Save with Lucia for a house deposit over the next two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see how it goes, and let's not rush. At work I'd go along with whatever the practice decided, but I'd want somebody to show me properly. I wouldn't be the one standing up at a meeting about it either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be worried about looking even slower. If the other doctors are letting the AI write letters and sort results, and I'm still typing with two fingers, that shows. But family medicine round here is a lot of talking and touching people, so I don't think the job disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see for the first few months, watch who uses what and whether it actually works. Then I'd ask Lucia to show me, because she uses an AI checker at the pharmacy for drug interactions and she's patient with me. I'd do the practice's training, once, properly, and stick with whatever bit actually saves me time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicking. Like starting a new rotation where everyone else already knows where the cupboards are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Millbrook would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret, who does the prescriptions and the repeat orders, because that's exactly the kind of checking and booking the AI does. She's been at the practice thirty years. She'd lose more to this than any doctor would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a few months. Isn't that risky when you're already slower?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've seen people jump on things and then have to unlearn them. I'd rather be three months behind and right than first and wrong. In a practice like ours, nobody's going to sack a doctor for being careful.

say: Let's **see how it goes** and not rush into anything.
I'd go along with the practice, but I'd want **proper training**.
think: I'm worried about looking **even slower** while others let AI write letters.
Family medicine here is **talking and touching** people, so the job stays.
do: Wait a **few months** to see which tools actually work.
Ask Lucia to show me her **pharmacy AI checker** first.
Do the practice's **training** once and keep only what saves time.
feel: **Uneasy**, like starting a rotation where everyone already knows the cupboards.
S1.quote: I'd rather be three months behind and right than first and wrong.
fieldNote: He'd lean on his **girlfriend** to learn the tools, not the practice.
He thinks the **prescriptions clerk** loses more than any doctor.
His caution is **deliberate**: he'd rather be late and right.

steps.text: Watch for three months which tools the other doctors keep using
Learn the AI letter writer with Lucia's help and the practice training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow down, we don't know if this is safe, and I'd mean it. I'd say patients in a town like ours want to see a face. Beyond that I'd keep my head down, I'm not a campaigner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me a bit. If the AI does the thinking part by 2028, that's the history, the diagnosis, the letters, which is most of what I'm slow at anyway. I'd be twenty-nine and only half-trained, and the one thing I'd still have is the hands-on part, the visits and examinations, which robots wouldn't do until around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch my training towards things you do with your hands. Maybe the minor injuries unit at the county hospital, stitching, setting fingers, plastering, because that buys me those three extra years. Lucia and I would put the house on hold and keep renting, and I'd keep the savings in the bank rather than spend them on a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like the ground's moving and I can't see where it stops. I've still got money and options, but I'd be thinking about it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lucia about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we wait. Her job is mostly checking prescriptions, so the AI hits her too, maybe harder than me. A doctor and a pharmacist both in jobs the AI can do by 2028 means it isn't the time to sign a twenty-five-year mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not a campaigner. Would that change at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, to be honest. I'd sign a petition if the practice put one up. But I'd spend my energy on learning to stitch and plaster, because that's what I can actually control.

say: We should **slow down**, because nobody knows if this is safe.
Patients in a town like ours want to **see a face**.
think: The AI takes the **thinking part** by 2028, which is most of what I'm slow at.
Only the **hands-on part** remains, and robots reach that around 2031.
do: Move my training towards the **minor injuries unit** at the county hospital.
Put the **house purchase** on hold and keep renting with Lucia.
Keep our **savings** in the bank instead of spending them on a deposit.
feel: **Anxious**, with the ground moving and no clear end in sight.
Steadied a little by having **money and options**.
S2.quote: A doctor and a pharmacist both in jobs the AI can do by 2028 means it isn't the time to sign a twenty-five-year mortgage.
fieldNote: Both earners face **thinking AI**, since his girlfriend is a pharmacist.
He plans to buy **three extra years** through hands-on skills like stitching.
He won't **campaign**, choosing to spend energy on what he can control.

steps.text: Apply for minor injuries training at the county hospital
Put the house purchase with Lucia on hold and keep renting
Keep the deposit savings in the bank as a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: go carefully and keep people in charge. With five years, I'd say the practices should be training us now, not in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes a real difference for me. I'd be fully trained by 2029 and thirty-two when it lands, with a couple of years as a proper family doctor behind me. The hands-on work would last until about 2034, and by then I'd have done minor surgery and the injuries work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish training and add the minor procedures along the way: joint injections, stitching, skin lesions. I'd probably learn the AI tools in the second or third year, once Millbrook had settled on the ones it trusts. And Lucia and I would still buy a house, just a cheaper one and later, maybe 2028, with a smaller mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd manage. Five years is enough to finish what I started. I'd stop thinking about it most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Millbrook look like by 2031, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer doctors, probably, and more nurses doing the visits with an AI on a tablet. Dr Halvorsen would have long retired. I'd want to be one of the doctors who still does the procedures and the difficult visits, the dying patients and the confused ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools in year two or three. Why not now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because now they change every six months and I'm slow. If I learn one now, I'll have to learn another next year. Better to learn whatever the practice finally settles on and learn it properly once.

say: Go **carefully** and keep people in charge of patients.
Practices should be **training us now**, not waiting until 2030.
think: I'd be **fully trained** by 2029 and thirty-two when AGI lands.
The **hands-on work** lasts until about 2034, by which time I'd have procedure skills.
do: Add **minor procedures** like joint injections and stitching during training.
Learn the AI tools in **year two or three**, once Millbrook settles.
Buy a **cheaper house** with Lucia later, around 2028.
feel: **Uneasy** but manageable, with five years enough to finish what he started.
S3.quote: I'd want to be one of the doctors who still does the procedures and the difficult visits, the dying patients and the confused ones.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **finish training**, which takes most of the fear away.
He wants the **difficult visits**: the dying and the confused.
He'd learn AI **once**, after the tools stop changing every six months.

steps.text: Add joint injections, stitching and skin lesion removal to his training
Learn whichever AI tools Millbrook settles on by his third year
Buy a cheaper house with Lucia around 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and a lot can change. I'd tell people not to panic and not to believe everyone who says they know what 2036 looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it's fine for a long while. I'd be thirty-seven in 2036, settled, maybe a partner at Millbrook. Ten years is enough time for me to work out the tools slowly, the way I like, and to see what other practices do first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd carry on as normal: training, house, visits. I'd keep an eye on it, maybe check once a year what's changed. I wouldn't do anything big until I could see it actually coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is ages. I'd worry about it when it's closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until you could see it coming. When would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably when the AI starts doing things at Millbrook that only doctors did, like deciding who needs a visit. Then I'd know it's real. Until then it's people on the news guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry when it's closer. Is there a risk in that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, there is. I know I can be lazy about change, and Lucia says so too. If I wait until 2035 to start learning anything, I'll be a thirty-six-year-old doctor learning from scratch. I don't want that.

say: Ten years is a **long time**, and a lot can change.
Don't **panic**, and don't believe anyone who claims to know 2036.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** and settled, maybe a partner at Millbrook, by 2036.
Ten years lets me learn the tools **slowly**, after other practices go first.
do: Carry on with **training, house and visits** as normal.
Check **once a year** what has changed in the practice.
Hold off on **big moves** until AI starts making doctors' decisions at Millbrook.
feel: **Calm**, because ten years feels like ages away.
S4.quote: If I wait until 2035 to start learning anything, I'll be a thirty-six-year-old doctor learning from scratch.
fieldNote: He admits he can be **lazy about change**, and his girlfriend agrees.
His signal to act is **AI deciding** who gets a home visit.
The long timeline suits his **wait-and-see** habit, with a risk he names himself.

steps.text: Carry on training, home visits and the house purchase as planned
Wait until AI starts deciding home visits at Millbrook before acting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be half-trained, slow on computers, and Lucia's job would be hit at the same time. What would help is a proper paid route into hands-on work like minor injuries, and someone patient to train people like me on the tools, not a two-hour online course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what towns like ours need. The city gets all the new things first, but out here people are older and they want someone they know. A town of retired farmers won't trust a tablet the way a city of students will.

headlineQuote: A town of retired farmers won't trust a tablet the way a city of students will.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old junior doctor** at Millbrook, a six-doctor practice in a market town of farmers and retired people.
He lives with Lucia, a **pharmacist**, and they're saving for a house deposit.
He's **slow on computers**, never uses AI tools, and prefers to wait until something is proven.
His mood runs from **calm to anxious**, worst with two-year AGI, which hits both his and Lucia's thinking work.
His plan is to move into **hands-on skills** like stitching and minor injuries, not to campaign.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when he'd be half-trained and his girlfriend's pharmacy job would be hit too.
whatWouldHelp: A paid route into **hands-on work** like minor injuries.
Patient, **in-person training** on the tools rather than a short online course.
